items.title: DialoStack: task-oriented spoken dialogue for ROS 2, with the LLM kept out of the control flow
items.summary: I’ve been working on getting a robot to run structured spoken conversations, things like a clinic intake (collect name, age, reason for the visit, allergies…), explaining a topic and checking the person understood it, or running a short quiz. Wiring an LLM straight into the speech loop gets you a nice demo quickly, but in my tests it was hard to rely on: it drifted off task, re-asked things it already had, or never decided the conversation was over. So I built DialoStack, a set of ROS 2 packages where the dialogue flow is plain Python (states, turn limits, confirmation, cancellation) and the LLM is only used to interpret what the user said and to phrase the next reply. It started as my bachelor’s thesis, and I presented the work at WAF 2026, the International Workshop on Physical Agents. I’ve put a lot of care into it and I don’t want it to end up as another thesis repo that nobody touches after graduation, so I’m releasing it as open source (MIT) and plan to keep working on it. Feedback from people doing HRI would help a lot. A slot-filling task in the web monitor: the frame on the right is filled turn by turn and confirmed before the action returns. Wiring an LLM straight into the speech loop gets you a nice demo quickly, but in my tests it was hard to rely on: it drifted off task, re-asked things it already had, or never decided the conversation was over. So I built DialoStack, a set of ROS 2 packages where the dialogue flow is plain Python (states, turn limits, confirmation, cancellation) and the LLM is only used to interpret what the user said and to phrase the next reply. It started as my bachelor’s thesis, and I presented the work at WAF 2026, the International Workshop on Physical Agents. I’ve put a lot of care into it and I don’t want it to end up as another thesis repo that nobody touches after graduation, so I’m releasing it as open source (MIT) and plan to keep working on it. Feedback from people doing HRI would help a lot. 4_captura_gui 1860×990 162 KB A slot-filling task in the web monitor: the frame on the right is filled turn by turn and confirmed before the action returns. Demo on a real NAO (4 min): Dropbox How it’s used Everything goes through one action. You describe the task, and if you don’t pass a schema the engine generates one: ros2 action send_goal --feedback /dialog/execute_task \ ros2_dialog_interfaces/action/DialogTask \ "{task_description: 'Take a coffee order: drink type, size and customer name', dialog_mode: 'slot_filling', domain: 'coffee shop'}" The robot asks for whatever is missing, handles corrections (“actually, make it a large”), confirms, and returns the filled frame as JSON in the result. You can also pass your own schema and a partially filled frame to resume an interrupted dialogue. There is a BehaviorTree.CPP leaf node that wraps the same action. What’s in the repo ros2_dialog_manager : the FSM and three strategies (slot filling, explanation, quiz), with a registry for adding new ones ros2_llm_manager : LLM inference as an action with per-dialogue sessions; Gemini or Ollama behind the same interface, so it can run fully local speech_io : faster-whisper + Silero VAD for STT, Piper for streaming TTS; the mic is muted while the robot speaks vision_io (optional): facial emotion and lip activity, published as topics and added to the prompt context robots/nao : talking gestures and eye-LED feedback, in RViz and on the real robot (via nao_lola) evaluation/ : ROS-free benchmarks against hand-annotated data (slot extraction P/R/F1, intent confusion matrix, quiz grading, simulated end-to-end dialogues) The deterministic core has 173 unit tests that run with plain pytest . Status and limitations ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04, built from source. No binaries yet. You don’t need a robot: a microphone and speakers are enough. Local models via Ollama work and keep all data on the machine, but small ones are noticeably less accurate than Gemini. The only embodiment layer so far is NAO. The core just publishes /is_speaking and /user_vad , so mapping those to another robot should be straightforward, but I haven’t done it. Related work llama_ros and whisper_ros provide LLM and STT inference as ROS 2 nodes, and ROS4HRI defines common HRI interfaces. DialoStack sits a level above those: it’s the dialogue management layer that decides what to ask next and when a task is done. In principle the STT and LLM nodes could be replaced by those packages, though I haven’t tried it yet. Feedback I’m looking for Does a single DialogTask action with a free-text task description feel like the right interface, or would you rather define dialogues declaratively (YAML, BT)? If you work with other social robots (Pepper, TIAGo, …), what would you need from the embodiment layer? Dialogue types you’d use that aren’t covered by slot filling / explanation / quiz. A few issues are tagged good first issue if anyone wants to contribute (an OpenAI-compatible provider, more TTS voices, tests for the quiz and explanation strategies). Bug reports are just as welcome: I’d rather hear what breaks than have it fail quietly on someone’s robot. Repo: GitHub - aquintan4/DialoStack: Task-oriented spoken dialogue for ROS 2 robots. I’m posting in Projects because it ships with a ROS 2 reference bridge and I want feedback from people who would actually wire it in. Up front: the core is not open source. It ships as a compiled package under an evaluation license; the repo holds docs, examples and the issue tracker. What it does It keeps task experience (an episode, where it failed, what a human did, what followed) with the source of every fact, and returns what is relevant when a later task asks under its current conditions. With a model key it drafts candidate lessons from that experience, which you review before they are used. New outcomes and counterexamples revise those lessons. Interfaces Local HTTP API on loopback: POST /v1/robots register a robot instance POST /v1/events:batch episodes and events (default cap 50 events / 1 MiB per batch) POST /v1/recall original source facts POST /v1/memory/recall reviewed task memory POST /v1/feedback whether the result was used, and what happened POST /v1/events/{event_id}/revoke withdraw a source event Python SDK over the same calls (register_robot , ingest , recall , recall_memory , feedback ). No NumPy dependency, so serialization is explicit. ExperienceJournal keeps the full episode locally, including delivery position, action intents and use feedback. If delivery fails, you reopen the journal and flush it explicitly. ROS 2 reference bridge: task-level DDS services, a persistent request queue and source-bound private configuration. Queue acceptance and host confirmation are separate steps. Exercised on Ubuntu 24.04 / Jazzy / ARM64 with real ROS processes. Simulation clock values keep their own domain; it does not invent UTC timestamps without a valid mapping. The bridge guide ships inside the install package. Gymnasium helper for ordinary single environments: reset info, seed, transitions, rewards and terminated vs truncated are preserved. VectorEnv, AutoReset and asynchronous multi-agent are not implemented. Why the feedback call exists: recall alone tells you nothing. Recording whether the planner used what came back, and what followed, is how you check whether memory changed behavior. Boundaries Perception, control, policy, execution permissions and e-stop stay with the integrator. It does not trigger motor actions. Missing memory or an unavailable service needs an application-defined fallback. No weight training. What gets revised is experience content and the conditions it applies under. JSON assets are capped at 2 MiB each. Images and video need your own asset manager; this interface does not do visual understanding. Model-assisted steps use your own Gemini key, called directly against Google and billed to you. Selected material goes to the model provider only with your explicit authorization. Install, experience write and source-fact recall work without a key. Try it without hardware examples/README.md in the repo has a synthetic Python example that registers a synthetic robot, ingests a short episode and recalls source facts. No model key, no control hardware. Platforms: Apple Silicon Mac (CPython 3.12); Linux ARM64 and AMD64 via OCI, with containerd/nerdctl as the tested path. ARM64 validated in an ARM VM; AMD64 so far under Rosetta translation, not yet on a physical AMD64 host. The local console is mostly Chinese for now; API, SDK and docs are English. Evaluation is free under the bundled license; model costs are separate. Site: Monolithos Robot Brain — Every task ends. Experience carries on. Repo: GitHub - silas-zhen/robot-brain: Persistent memory for embodied AI. Source-backed experience for robot planning, recovery and training review. · GitHub Bring one real task boundary: a failure, a human correction, or the moment before the next plan. Run experience write and recall first, then decide where memory should take part in the decision. We want to build the experience interface and the ways experience gets used together with embodied AI teams. Integration guide: docs/en/integration.md in the repo. Tell us your task: the integration request template under the repo’s Issues. For those running ROS 2 on hardware or in long sim campaigns: where would you call recall? Before the planner, inside a recovery behavior tree, or only in offline review? And which of the bridge’s assumptions would break first on your setup? The goal is to reduce reliance on dedicated welding fixtures by using one robot to grip and hold the workpiece while another welds it. video: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/986d984e-00fb-4769-97a7-4cb6e9866428 The grasping and welding components can also be used independently. The framework combines constraint-aware grasp sampling, weld seam extraction from CAD/mesh geometry, and motion planning with MoveIt 2. It targets ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04. It’s currently a proof of concept demonstrated in simulation. Repository hold_and_weld_050 1920×1080 248 KB Constraint-aware grasp sampling The grasp sampler generates antipodal grasp candidates on exact CAD surfaces. Exclusion volumes keep grasps away from weld seams, screw holes and other forbidden regions. Candidates are filtered using gripper geometry and checked for collisions with the workpiece, secondary objects and the ground. STEP and URDF inputs are supported. hold_and_weld_141 1920×1080 220 KB Weld seam extraction The weld finder extracts seams from CAD and mesh geometry and exports weld paths as JSON. The mesh pipeline identifies contact boundaries between parts, traces them along the parts’ edges, and refines the resulting weld paths. hold_and_weld_272 1920×1080 201 KB Weld approach configuration and motion planning Reaching the start of a seam does not necessarily give the robot a suitable configuration for completing the weld. ConfigurationFinder selects the approach joint configuration before OMPL plans the approach. A custom Ceres-based IK solver minimizes position and orientation errors, with hard joint bounds and a seed penalty that favors configurations close to the seed. Multiple initial seeds explore alternative IK branches. Each candidate is evaluated along a sampled Cartesian path covering the plunge and weld motion. IK is solved at each sample using the previous solution as the seed. Candidates are rejected on IK failure, joint-limit violations, low Yoshikawa manipulability or excessive joint steps. Feasible candidates are ranked by their minimum joint-limit margin, minimum manipulability and distance from the home configuration. OMPL plans to the selected configuration as a joint goal. Pilz handles the plunge and linear/circular weld motions; other curves use a dense-waypoint Cartesian fallback. Dual-arm coordination Action servers handle grasping and welding, while a coordinator sequences the workcell: the gripper arm picks and holds the workpiece, then the welding arm executes the weld path. Separate launch files allow either side to run independently. Robot and gripper catalog Models and robot base poses are selected through workcell.yaml . Additional robot and gripper models can be easily integrated through xacro wrappers and catalog registration. A guide documents the required interfaces and configuration steps. Configurator and visualizers The workcell configurator lets you select robot and gripper models and position robots and scene objects using interactive markers in RViz2. Layouts are saved as YAML files, which can be copied into the workcell configuration. Separate visualizers display grasp candidates and weld paths. Testing and current limitations The repository includes unit tests. I also created a complex geometry example with concavities, elliptical surfaces and other geometric features to test grasp sampling and seam extraction. Results look good on the tested examples; additional geometry testing would help assess broader coverage. The complete workflow has been demonstrated in simulation. It has not yet been validated through physical welding trials. Existing physical demonstrations show that robot-held welding is feasible at smaller scales too. I’m actively working toward a hardware demonstration of this framework. The roadmap outlines planned development. Installation and documentation Prebuilt Docker image: docker pull ghcr.io/silanus23/hold_and_weld:0.3.0 The repository includes installation instructions, usage examples, package documentation and a guide for adding robot and gripper models. items.articleText: EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model Oct 06, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link EmbeddingGemma 2 is the most capable model for on-device multimodal embeddings, natively mapping combinations of text, images, audio, and video into a unified embedding space. Sahil Dua Research Engineer, Google DeepMind Henrique Schechter Vera Research Engineer, Google DeepMind Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X We introduced EmbeddingGemma last year to provide a lightweight option for high-quality text embeddings, to help your apps organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware. The developer community’s response blew past our expectations. With more than 20 million downloads, builders have used it to power smarter on-device search tools and privacy-first retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipelines. Today, we’re launching EmbeddingGemma 2, expanding beyond text to unify code, images, video, and audio in a shared embedding space. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license, EmbeddingGemma 2 has 740 million parameters, making it optimal for on-device inference. It can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model. Built from the same technology as Gemini Embedding models, EmbeddingGemma 2 is: Best-in-class for its size: Achieves leading scores among sub-1B multimodal embedders for its size across benchmarks like MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) Code and MAEB (Massive Audio Embedding Benchmark), while matching or outperforming many larger models across text, vision, and audio tasks. Modular by design: Requires as little as 270M parameters for text-only workloads with optional vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders for full multimodal support. Storage-efficient: Using Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), developers can dynamically truncate output vectors from 768 dimensions down to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions. This provides up to 6x storage reduction for local vector databases and memory usage. Optimized for on-device performance: Runs efficiently within tight resource constraints. With quantization, on a Google Pixel 11 Pro, EmbeddingGemma 2 requires as little as ~191MB active RAM for text-only weights and ~567MB for the full multimodal model. Extended context ready: Features an 8K token context window (4x larger than EmbeddingGemma 1), allowing it to process up to 5.5 minutes of audio, 29 images, 58 video frames, or interleaved combinations thereof directly on local hardware. Achieving top-tier quality for code, vision, and audio EmbeddingGemma 2 matches the strong multilingual text performance of EmbeddingGemma while delivering a significant 9.92-point improvement on code performance (in MTEB Code, from 68.76 to 78.68), making it well-suited for local codebase indexing, semantic code search, and coding agent retrieval. Across image, video, documents, and audio, it sets a new standard in quality-per-parameter for sub-1B models and even outperforms some specialist models more than twice its size. Find full evaluation metrics and model information in the EmbeddingGemma 2 model card . Enabling semantic search, routing, and retrieval, fully on-device EmbeddingGemma 2 brings robust capabilities directly to edge hardware. Generating embeddings locally helps ensure data privacy, reduces pipeline latency, and empowers developers to build cross-modal search and retrieval that works entirely offline. When paired with generative models such as Gemma 4, EmbeddingGemma 2 enables on-device RAG pipelines that understand complex multimodal data. Because EmbeddingGemma 2 is built on Gemma 4 and shares its text tokenizer and audio encoder, developers can run both models together in a unified pipeline with a lower combined total memory footprint. Use text or an image to find the top matches in your media library based on semantic similarity. Try it in Google AI Edge Gallery ’s Instant Media Search. Locate specific moments in video using text or audio queries. Try it in Google AI Edge Gallery ’s Video Moments Finder. Pair EmbeddingGemma 2 for local file retrieval with Gemma 4 for contextual reasoning. Try it in the Google AI Edge Foresight app. Create real-time decision engines leveraging multimodal context for classification, routing, and predictive capabilities via the MediaPipe Decision Task API . To learn how to build on-device search and RAG systems with LiteRT, read the Google AI Edge blog post . Getting started with EmbeddingGemma 2 We worked closely with the following partners to ensure EmbeddingGemma 2 works immediately where you build: Download the models: Find the model weights on Hugging Face and Kaggle , with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden availability coming soon. Visit LiteRT Community on Hugging Face for models optimized for on-device. On-device deployment: Develop cross-platform apps with Google AI Edge MediaPipe for turnkey embedding, retrieval & decision tasks or LiteRT for custom model integration. Build for the browser with transformers.js or WebGPU . Use your favorite development tools : Serve the model efficiently using transformers, sentence-transformers, MLX , vLLM, llama.cpp , SGLang, Ollama , and LMStudio. Store your embedding vectors with Qdrant . Fine-tuning: Follow guidance by Unsloth for how to fine-tune EmbeddingGemma 2 for your use cases. Explore our developer guide , documentation , and guides for inference and fine-tuning . items.title: EmbeddingGemma 2
items.summary: My comment on EmbeddingGemma 2 — Hacker News. I really appreciate that EmbeddingGemma 2 is under the Apache 2.0 license. For embedding models in particular, I don't think it makes sense to use a closed, proprietary, hosted-only model. Most applications of embedding models involve calculating thousands or even millions of embedding vectors and storing them for later comparison. If your model is proprietary, the vendor is likely someday going to decide to stop offering that model. They'll have a better model to replace it, but you still need to pay to re-calculate those millions of stored existing vectors. (In April 2024 OpenAI offered to "cover the financial cost of users re-embedding content with these new models" - https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-api-general-availability/ - but I don't think that's something we can rely on from every provider.) Notably, I don't want to host the model myself . I'd much rather pay a provider for a hosted model while knowing that if they ever stop hosting it I can run the open weights version myself - or find another vendor who can do that for me. items.title: Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk
items.summary: Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk Mistral are back in the game. Today they're releasing a preview of Mistral Large 4, a 1 trillion parameter, 49 billion active parameter model trained on their own cluster of 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The preview is available via their API. They promise to release the open weights model at the "end of this month". The model only supports two reasoning levels - "none" and "high" - via the Mistral API. Here are both pelicans - the "high" one looks better, though surprisingly it only used 2,717 output tokens compared to "none" which used 3,275: On Artificial Analysis it scores 38 , just behind DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, which is a 552B model. It's a huge improvement on last December's Mistral Large 3, which drew this terrible pelican and scored 9 on AA . It's certainly not a Fable-class model, but it's great to see Mistral put out a model that's back to being maybe about 6 months behind the frontier. It's a huge improvement on last December's Mistral Large 3, which drew this terrible pelican and scored 9 on AA . It's certainly not a Fable-class model, but it's great to see Mistral put out a model that's back to being maybe about 6 months behind the frontier. items.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: An open, lightweight multimodal embedding model
items.articleText: EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model Oct 06, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link EmbeddingGemma 2 is the most capable model for on-device multimodal embeddings, natively mapping combinations of text, images, audio, and video into a unified embedding space. Sahil Dua Research Engineer, Google DeepMind Henrique Schechter Vera Research Engineer, Google DeepMind Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X We introduced EmbeddingGemma last year to provide a lightweight option for high-quality text embeddings, to help your apps organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware. The developer community’s response blew past our expectations. With more than 20 million downloads, builders have used it to power smarter on-device search tools and privacy-first retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipelines. Today, we’re launching EmbeddingGemma 2, expanding beyond text to unify code, images, video, and audio in a shared embedding space. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license, EmbeddingGemma 2 has 740 million parameters, making it optimal for on-device inference. It can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model. Built from the same technology as Gemini Embedding models, EmbeddingGemma 2 is: Best-in-class for its size: Achieves leading scores among sub-1B multimodal embedders for its size across benchmarks like MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) Code and MAEB (Massive Audio Embedding Benchmark), while matching or outperforming many larger models across text, vision, and audio tasks. Modular by design: Requires as little as 270M parameters for text-only workloads with optional vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders for full multimodal support. Storage-efficient: Using Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), developers can dynamically truncate output vectors from 768 dimensions down to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions. This provides up to 6x storage reduction for local vector databases and memory usage. Optimized for on-device performance: Runs efficiently within tight resource constraints. With quantization, on a Google Pixel 11 Pro, EmbeddingGemma 2 requires as little as ~191MB active RAM for text-only weights and ~567MB for the full multimodal model. Extended context ready: Features an 8K token context window (4x larger than EmbeddingGemma 1), allowing it to process up to 5.5 minutes of audio, 29 images, 58 video frames, or interleaved combinations thereof directly on local hardware. Achieving top-tier quality for code, vision, and audio EmbeddingGemma 2 matches the strong multilingual text performance of EmbeddingGemma while delivering a significant 9.92-point improvement on code performance (in MTEB Code, from 68.76 to 78.68), making it well-suited for local codebase indexing, semantic code search, and coding agent retrieval. Across image, video, documents, and audio, it sets a new standard in quality-per-parameter for sub-1B models and even outperforms some specialist models more than twice its size. Find full evaluation metrics and model information in the EmbeddingGemma 2 model card . Enabling semantic search, routing, and retrieval, fully on-device EmbeddingGemma 2 brings robust capabilities directly to edge hardware. Generating embeddings locally helps ensure data privacy, reduces pipeline latency, and empowers developers to build cross-modal search and retrieval that works entirely offline. When paired with generative models such as Gemma 4, EmbeddingGemma 2 enables on-device RAG pipelines that understand complex multimodal data. Because EmbeddingGemma 2 is built on Gemma 4 and shares its text tokenizer and audio encoder, developers can run both models together in a unified pipeline with a lower combined total memory footprint. Use text or an image to find the top matches in your media library based on semantic similarity. Try it in Google AI Edge Gallery ’s Instant Media Search. Locate specific moments in video using text or audio queries. Try it in Google AI Edge Gallery ’s Video Moments Finder. Pair EmbeddingGemma 2 for local file retrieval with Gemma 4 for contextual reasoning. Try it in the Google AI Edge Foresight app. Create real-time decision engines leveraging multimodal context for classification, routing, and predictive capabilities via the MediaPipe Decision Task API . To learn how to build on-device search and RAG systems with LiteRT, read the Google AI Edge blog post . Getting started with EmbeddingGemma 2 We worked closely with the following partners to ensure EmbeddingGemma 2 works immediately where you build: Download the models: Find the model weights on Hugging Face and Kaggle , with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden availability coming soon. Visit LiteRT Community on Hugging Face for models optimized for on-device. On-device deployment: Develop cross-platform apps with Google AI Edge MediaPipe for turnkey embedding, retrieval & decision tasks or LiteRT for custom model integration. Build for the browser with transformers.js or WebGPU . Use your favorite development tools : Serve the model efficiently using transformers, sentence-transformers, MLX , vLLM, llama.cpp , SGLang, Ollama , and LMStudio. Store your embedding vectors with Qdrant . Fine-tuning: Follow guidance by Unsloth for how to fine-tune EmbeddingGemma 2 for your use cases. LLMs may have helped my RSI
items.articleText: October 05, 2026 Posts LLMs may have immensely helped my RSI I was playing piano for the first time in a while the other day and noticed: I didn’t feel any RSI. Maybe a bit and some tenderness, but not much at all. And no, I don’t mean recursive self improvement that is so trendy and topical right now. You see, for many years (starting as early as 2017) I had suffered some form of repetitive strain injury from as far as my doctors and I could tell was from simply typing on a keyboard and using my keyboard simply too much. I was learning to play piano, as you can imagine from the prior passage. This all added up to quite the strain on my arms at the end of the day. There has been good periods and bad periods since that time, but I remember coming home some days and my forearms would just be absolutely burning . The pain is the sort that you don’t forget. You experience it and never forget. I even read books such as “The Mindbody Prescription: Healing the Body, Healing the Pain” to try and reduce this. You don’t start reading books for treating your pain; you grasp at them because you’re desperate. I learned through the years to manage this, exercise more and take more breaks. I had gotten the pain down to some periods of 0-2 a month at most and tried all the usual stuff: ergonomic keyboards, more breaks, less time at a keyboard and various other techniques. Many of these things helped a lot but going a full day could be quite the task if it was a particularly heavy day. I also learned to type on home row retraining years of bad habits when I realized the some of the strain was coming from moving my wrist all over the keyboard and not keeping things straight. So, all this to say that I came a long way from the weekly pain that I would be experiencing that was quite a burning feeling. But the most noticeable days of pain had something in common: the types of keys I would be striking. You see, I would be able to type 20 pages of a design document with some rest in-between and not feel much at all. Sure, I might have some soreness from striking the keys (and still do, after writing a post like this one I may need some small breaks in between if not using voice dictation). But this was nothing compared to the days where I would write code for 4-5 hours in a stretch. This was even more common when I was a junior. This would normally involve trying to type special characters all over the keyboard. Hitting angled brackets, hitting various FN keys, striking home, end, tons of modifier keys, contorting my wrist in all sorts of ways that I really should not be. This was part of the motivation to learn to type “the right way”: to reduce these types of problems. Probably something that made it worse is that my hands are much smaller than average as a male. My finger span could barely reach an octave if I tried and much more than this is tough: So, yeah. Small hands. I had similar problems raiding in Final Fantasy XIV and never really thought about it much until I started talking with some of my raid members and realized they were using combos that would involve Ctrl and up to the number 5! I cannot make that reach without some serious stretching that you can definitely feel. Something changed slowly in 2026 though. I still write quite a bit of code by hand when it’s called for and needed. But increasingly, more code is being written by agents. When I want to do small refactors that are mechanical, I simply ask for then. An entire feature that I might write out in the afternoon which could span 4 - 5 hours of typing and debugging are replaced with prompts and maybe 30 minutes of manual refinement. I spend more time writing good design specifications and reviewing that of others. I review more code, but I am typing more on home row as a result. I might actually write more character per character than I used to but I am spending less time all over the keyboard and more time just typing… English prose. All that fits in the span of my fingertips. It is also probably true that I spent more time in meetings which is a natural consequence of becoming more senior. But to be clear: I shipped more code this year probably than any other year before it (I’m working on a greenfield product, working in Healthcare prior it was a different story). I woke the other day thinking: hmm, I’ve not felt some arm pain in any serious capacity in quite some time. That’s interesting. I’ve felt some fatigue, sure. I mentioned that in my recent post talking about my new Macbook Air here . But serious, burning pain? It’s been quite some time! Perhaps it could be because I simply spend more time writing essays rather than moving my hands all over a keyboard pecking at keys. I have my own set of complicated feelings of LLMs (gone are the bouts of satisfaction I would get hammering out code in an afternoon and watching it work at the end of the day). However, it seems increasingly more likely that from a health perspective perhaps they have been a boon to me. Or perhaps I am just senior enough now that it’s no longer a problem. At any rate, if the machines ultimately let me live a healthier life, then so be it. Without your health, you are nothing after all. ## What's Changed

**Models run on MLX on Apple Silicon by default**

In this release, on Apple Silicon devices, model architectures supported by the MLX runtime will automatically run on MLX.

```
ollama pull qwen3.8
ollama run qwen3.8
```

Additional models include [gemma4](https://ollama.com/library/gemma4), [qwen3.6](https://ollama.com/library/qwen3.6) and [qwen3.5](https://ollama.com/library/qwen3.5)

We will continue testing and enabling additional models.

items.title: Boston Dynamics appoints former Amazon exec Rohit Prasad as new CEO
items.summary: Before Boston Dynamics, Prasad served as senior vice president and head scientist for Alexa and artificial general intelligence at Amazon. The post Boston Dynamics appoints former Amazon exec Rohit Prasad as new CEO appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Rohit Prasad is Boston Dynamics’ new CEO. | Source: Boston Dynamics It’s been nearly nine months since Robert Playter, the former CEO of Boston Dynamics, stepped down. The company today named Rohit Prasad as its new CEO, effective tomorrow. Prasad will take over from Chief Financial Officer Amanda McMaster, who served as interim CEO after Playter left in February. Prior to joining Boston Dynamics, Prasad served as senior vice president and head scientist for Alexa and artificial general intelligence at Amazon. Boston Dynamics said Prasad’s appointment accelerates its physical AI strategy by combining robotics with advanced AI capabilities to commercialize intelligent machines at scale. “Boston Dynamics is uniquely positioned to advance physical AI through its world-class robotics expertise,” stated Prasad. “I am honored to join the company at such a pivotal moment for the industry. By bringing together advanced AI and robotics, we can build intelligent systems that create meaningful value in real-world environments, expand the reach of robotics across industries, and shape the next era of physical AI.” Prasad said he plans to productize intelligent robotic systems that improve safety, productivity, and operational efficiency across real-world industrial and commercial environments. Subject to the relevant approval process, Prasad is also expected to join the company ‘s Board of Directors. He is Boston Dynamics’ third CEO ever. Before Playter , founder Marc Raibert served as CEO from the company’s creation in 1992 until 2020 . Prasad has AI and robotics experience During Prasad’s 12 years at Amazon , he helped build Alexa from its earliest days into a pioneering large-scale consumer AI service. Now, people are using Alexa in hundreds of millions of households worldwide. More recently, he led the development of the Amazon Nova foundation model family used by enterprises. Before Amazon, Prasad spent nearly 14 years at Raytheon BBN Technologies. There, he lead machine-learning research and its real-world application for U.S. government and commercial use. “Boston Dynamics’ industry-leading robotics, Rohit’s proven ability to turn AI into products at global scale, and Hyundai Motor Group’s modern manufacturing , logistics , and mobility capabilities give us a powerful foundation to build and scale physical AI,” said Jaehoon Chang, the vice chair of Hyundai and chair of the board of directors at Boston Dynamics. “We are thrilled to welcome Rohit to lead the company into this exciting new era of real-world physical AI.” Hyundai acquired a controlling stake in the company from SoftBank Group in 2021. Boston Dynamics shares updates on Atlas, Spot It’s been a busy time for Boston Dynamics’ team. Last week, it unveiled the newest hand for the Atlas humanoid . The company said it built the the four-fingered hand, which doesn’t have a pinky finger, for high-fidelity simulation to enable sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL). A week before, Boston Dynamics opened its Robotics Metaplant Application Center (RMAC) at Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America. The Georgia facility is a training center for integrating Atlas into parent Hyundai’s automotive manufacturing operations. In addition, the company has introduced Spot 5.2 , the latest update to its quadruped robot platform. The new release enables Spot to use agentic workflows that reason across systems. Orbit AIVI, now powered by Google Gemini, extends this further by increasing the types of inspections Spot can perform. Boston Dynamics also makes the Stretch trailer-unloading robot and plans to spend $100 million expanding its facilities in Waltham, Mass. items.title: Pegasus 1.6 brings video understanding to physical AI, says TwelveLabs
items.summary: TwelveLabs says its Pegasus 1.6 model understands first-person video and supports workflows including labeling for robotics developers. The post Pegasus 1.6 brings video understanding to physical AI, says TwelveLabs appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Pegasus provides temporal context, spatial reasoning, and judgement on whether a task was completed. Source: TwelveLabs As the physical world rapidly digitalizes, AI teams are gathering vast amounts of complex video, but transforming raw footage into actionable models remains a critical challenge, according to TwelveLabs Inc. The company today released its Pegasus 1.6 model with added capabilities for understanding and navigating complex real-world environments. “Our mission has always been to help machines understand how the world works through video,” stated Jae Lee, co-founder and CEO of TwelveLabs. “Physical AI is the next expression of that mission. Most of what people know about doing physical work, such as a changing grip or a recovery after something slips, has never been captured in a form a machine can learn from.” “With our newest model release, we can now turn that footage into structured, reviewable knowledge, so robotics and physical AI teams can train on real human experience instead of starting from scratch,” he added. Founded in 2021, TwelveLabs said it has created a “full-stack video intelligence platform” using its Marengo and Pegasus models, which it designed to see and understand video the way humans do in a fraction of the time. Developers can use this single system that gets smarter over time to access and act on all of their video content, said the Seoul-based company . Pegasus 1.6 focuses on egocentric video TwelveLabs said its latest version of Pegasus marks its expansion into physical AI , generating rich insights from real-world perspectives. It solves workflow-specific challenges so that machines such as robots, drones, and autonomous vehicles can perceive, reason, and safely act in the physical world like never before, the company claimed. “We’re focused on the video understanding layer,” Jae Lee told The Robot Report . “You can’t just take millions of hours of video and feed it into a robotics model and expect useful training data to come out. You first need to understand what’s happening in the video, what action is taking place, when it happens, what the person is interacting with, how the behavior changes over time, and when other people or bystanders appear in the field of view.” “Pegasus 1.6 provides that more precise understanding so robotics and data teams can then turn it into the training data they need,” he added. TwelveLabs noted that Pegasus 1.6 is its first AI model built to understand egocentric video , which is shot from the point of view of the person doing the work. This could be someone cooking a meal, assembling parts on a factory line, or operating a robot remotely. The model does not require specific cameras, said Lee. “We’re not requiring robotics teams to use a particular camera or proprietary hardware to capture that footage,” he said. “What matters is being able to capture the actions and interactions taking place from the operator’s point of view.” In addition, Pegasus 1.6 can work with existing video data and allows for analysis of still images in addition to video. “One of the reasons we’re focused on egocentric video is that it’s much easier to collect and scale than teleoperation data,” acknowledged Lee. “The goal is to take that footage and make it more useful for robotics teams by identifying the actions taking place, breaking them into precise time segments and capturing finer-grained details about the behavior.” Head-mounted footage can break models trained on broadcast, instructional, and cinematic video. Source: TwelveLabs TwelveLabs supports five workflows Pegasus 1.6 currently supports five workflows powered by its video-native model. They include: Action segmentation and labeling: This feature accelerates model training with standardized datasets by automatically generating precise, time-stamped action labels for tasks, steps, objects, and hand-object interactions from raw video, mapped to the customer’s domain-specific taxonomy. Dense caption labeling: This enables natural language understanding for robots by producing rich, descriptive language for spatial relationships, scene context, and hand-object interactions to train advanced language-conditioned robot policies. Quality scoring: Users can save time by filtering out low-quality video by automatically evaluating and scoring video clips for action clarity, framing, and stability before sending footage to human reviewers. Search and curation: Customers can uncover critical edge cases by surfacing rare events, long-tail scenarios, and duplicate clips across an entire video repository using simple, natural-language search queries. Consent and compliance flagging: Privacy and compliance can be maintained by detecting and flagging faces, bystanders, and sensitive onscreen or paper data before video footage enters downstream development pipelines. Editor’s note: Physical AI is among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! Customers to benefit from existing capabilities Pegasus 1.6 builds on the video understanding capabilities that TwelveLabs developed for enterprises that maintain massive video libraries. The new release extends Pegasus 1.5’s functionality that attracted several new customers. TwelveLabs cited Time-Based Metadata (TBM), which allows users to define a custom schema and automatically receive timestamped, structured metadata from video content. This is particularly useful in aiding contextual understanding, as people often narrate what they are doing in egocentric clips, it said. Pegasus 1.6 has also improved entity recognition for more consistent tracking of hands, objects, and tools across clips. The model also offers faster, more cost-efficient processing for high-volume video workloads, according to TwelveLabs. Lee said that TwelveLabs’ system adds video understanding to other sensor modalities. “We’re focused on understanding the behavior we can observe in the video,” he said. “Pegasus 1.6 can identify the action taking place, segment it precisely in time, understand what the left and right hands are doing, and how the surrounding environment is changing.” “We can also provide a coarse understanding of how the limbs are moving based on the video, but we’re not trying to replace the robot’s tactile or actuator -level sensing,” he added. “Our role is to give robotics teams a richer understanding of the behavior in the video that they can combine with their own sensor data to build more precise trajectories and learning policies.” TwelveLabs said that Pegasus 1.6 expands on its existing collaborations with robotics developers. “We’re working with robotics labs and data teams that are using video to help scale the data available for robot training,” said Lee. “A lot of the work is focused on dexterity and manipulation, tasks like packaging , assembly , and cleaning , as well as more specialized industrial applications such as semiconductor quality control. The broader goal is to help these teams make much larger amounts of human behavioral video useful for training, which is far more scalable than teleoperation data.” About The Author Eugene Demaitre Eugene Demaitre is editorial director of the robotics group at Arrowfly (previously WTWH Media). He was senior editor of The Robot Report from 2019 to 2020 and editorial director of Robotics 24/7 from 2020 to 2023. Prior to working at Arrowfly, Demaitre was an editor at BNA (now part of Bloomberg), Computerworld, TechTarget, and Robotics Business Review. Demaitre has participated in robotics webcasts, podcasts, and conferences worldwide. He has a master's from the George Washington University and lives in the Boston area. Tell Us What You Think! items.title: Sovereign AI, same landlord — thoughts on the physical AI race
items.summary: While physical AI architecture alternatives are growing in number, NVIDIA has taken a sovereign strategy to ensuring its role. The post Sovereign AI, same landlord — thoughts on the physical AI race appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: NVIDIA has partnered with Hugging Face to ensure its role in physical AI development. Source: NVIDIA The physical AI developers determined not to rely on NVIDIA have had some wins lately. OpenAI shipped its own chip. Anthropic stood up an in-house silicon team with salaries that make FAANG recruiters wince. Also, Advanced Micro Devices acquired World Labs for $8.2 billion, Qualcomm has collaborated with Liquid AI on embedded agents, and Skild AI launched the S1 foundation model. In addition, Google DeepMind integrated Gemini Robotics 2 into Apptronik ‘s Apollo 2 humanoid. And then, almost politely, NVIDIA said it plans to spend $12.9 billion — the biggest acquisition in the company ‘s history — buying Hugging Face, the place where the planet’s developers go to pick which model to run. Cute war. NVIDIA just bought the battlefield. Chasing chips focuses on the wrong layer Several headlines have read “Labs race to cut NVIDIA loose.” Adorable framing. Here’s the actual scoreboard: While everyone else designed chips, NVIDIA designed an exit ramp that leads straight back to it, no matter which chip wins. That’s not defense. That’s a company that already read the ending and is waiting, patiently, for the rest of the industry to catch up. The chip numbers are genuinely impressive, to be fair. OpenAI spent nine months with Broadcom on Jalapeño. It is reportedly the fastest tape-out in the history of advanced semiconductors, shipping by year’s end. Anthropic followed with its own silicon team , posting hardware roles at up to $485,000, stacked on a multi-gigawatt Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) deal it already had running with Google and Broadcom. Google has had TPUs for a decade. AWS has Trainium . Meta has MTIA . Everyone is racing to stop writing Jensen Huang a check. None of these very expensive chips touch the place where the other 200,000 companies that will never build their own silicon actually go to find, fine-tune, and ship a model. That layer — the real on-ramp for the rest of the world’s AI adoption — just got quietly annexed by the company everyone claims to be staging a jailbreak from. NVIDIA didn’t flinch; it bought the prison. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! ‘Sovereign’ a clue to NVIDIA’s strategy Notice the word NVIDIA has kept reaching for in every earnings call so far this year: “sovereigns.” Not developers first. Not enterprises first. Sovereigns — nation-states spending public money on “AI independence” so they’re not permanently on their knees to a handful of U.S. labs. No government building sovereign AI wants to bet its national compute on OpenAI’s chip, Anthropic’s silicon, or any single lab that might someday become a geopolitical liability. So NVIDIA stepped in with the pitch: “Don’t worry, we’re neutral. Pick any model, any framework, any cloud you like” — a rousing speech about freedom of choice, delivered by the company that just bought the store where all the choices live. That’s the actual chess move. OpenAI and Anthropic are optimizing their own cost of goods. NVIDIA is optimizing for sitting underneath everyone’s cost of goods, forever, regardless of who wins the fight it’s graciously letting other people have. Nobody at Nvidia will ever put that in an earnings call. They don’t have to. The acquisition makes the argument for them. Here’s the part nobody wants to say out loud: Even a great custom chip takes years to match the volume, yield, and software maturity of a platform NVIDIA has spent two decades pouring into CUDA . Jalapeño’s nine-month tape-out is a real engineering flex. But by every account, it’s still a narrow inference chip built for OpenAI’s own workloads — not a platform anyone else is building a business on top of. Anthropic’s silicon team is, charitably, a hiring page with a mission statement, sitting inside a “multi-chip strategy” that still runs mostly on NVIDIA and Google hardware today. Meanwhile, NVIDIA just bolted on a distribution channel with Hugging Face that gets more daily developer traffic than either lab’s entire platform combined. NVIDIA says it has the most repos and the second-most homegrown models on Hugging Face. Source: Hugging Face Sovereign implications get sharper for robotics The implication gets sharper in physical AI. A robot cannot wait for a distant API to deliberate while it navigates a warehouse, handles sensitive equipment, or makes a safety-critical decision on a factory floor. It needs local inference, real-time control, sensor data that stays inside the operation, and a deployment stack that does not collapse because a cloud region hiccupped or a vendor changed its terms. That is precisely where “sovereign” stops being a procurement slogan and becomes an operational requirement. But the same landlord problem follows the robot onto the factory floor. The company that owns the training stack, simulation environment, edge runtime, developer tools, and model marketplace is not merely selling silicon—it is setting the terms for how physical intelligence gets built and deployed. Physical AI makes hardware choice matter more, not less. It also makes genuine portability across models, compute, and deployment environments far more valuable. None of this changes much for the companies shipping product to customers — if anything, it sharpens the point. Airrived last month launched its own sovereign AI platform, positioning itself as the agentic OS on a mission to democratize AI and turn every business user into an AI expert. That’s the other, more literal definition of “sovereign” — not a government hedging its national compute bet on a chip vendor, but a business user who doesn’t need a data center, a silicon roadmap, or a forward-deployed engineer to own and run their AI. NVIDIA’s version of sovereignty comes with a landlord attached. The application-layer version doesn’t care whose logo is silk-screened onto the silicon underneath it. It cares whether inference is fast, cheap, and boringly reliable, and it is happy to let $2 trillion-adjacent companies fight over who eats the infrastructure bill. That’s the quiet advantage of building lean above the war instead of funding a side in it: The chip fight is enormously expensive to win and completely free to ignore. Down where the silicon actually gets baked, this isn’t shaping up to be the underdog story the press releases want it to be. OpenAI and Anthropic are spending billions to buy independence from NVIDIA’s hardware. NVIDIA just spent $12.9 billion buying insurance against ever losing either of them — by owning the exact place their models must show up regardless of what chip runs them. Call it a war if you want. From here, it looks like NVIDIA collecting rent on both sides of the battlefield, smiling, and asking if anyone else would like to diversify. items.articleText: Telecom operators are increasingly building their AI strategies on open models — and the reasons go beyond mere cost. Open models give telcos the ability to trust, control and customize AI across their most critical workloads — from autonomous networks to customer care. NVIDIA’s latest State of AI in Telecommunications report reflects this shift, with 89% of respondents reporting that open source models and software are important to their company’s AI strategy. For operators, the strategic value of open models is fivefold: They expand access to frontier‑level intelligence at lower cost, allowing operators to reserve closed models for the workloads where they drive the most value. Independent benchmarks such as the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 show that leading open models are becoming more competitive across demanding reasoning, coding, scientific and agentic workloads. They support telco‑specific customization, with open weights and training recipes that operators can fine‑tune for their own operations using network, customer and industry data. They enable trustworthy AI by giving telcos greater visibility into and control over model artifacts and behavior, so models can be evaluated, adapted and governed in alignment with regulations and business policies. They enable flexible, secure deployment: teams can size and optimize open models to run across public clouds, private infrastructure and edge environments. They unlock the opportunity for telcos to deliver locally adapted AI services to enterprise and government customers by hosting and fine-tuning open models. Open Foundations, Tuned for Telecom Operations The NVIDIA Nemotron family of open models provides frontier -level reasoning performance optimized for agentic workflows, as well as speech capabilities for voice applications, with open weights, training data and recipes. SoftBank Corp. illustrates how an operator can use open models as a basis for developing and continuously advancing its telecom-specific AI capabilities. “Open models allow SoftBank Corp. to build on the rapid progress of global foundation models while applying the network knowledge and operational expertise we have accumulated over many years,” said Rajeev Koodli, principal fellow of SoftBank Corp. and senior vice president of SB Telecom America. “We are using open foundations extensively, including NVIDIA Nemotron models and others, in developing our SoftBank Large Telecom Model, continuously advancing it for telecom-specific use cases such as network operations, design and overall management.” In addition, NVIDIA is collaborating with partners to help turn open models into practical building blocks for telecom AI. NVIDIA announced the 30-billion-parameter Nemotron 3 Large Telco Model (LTM), fine-tuned by AdaptKey on open source telecom datasets to deliver accuracy gains for telecom-specific tasks. This gives operators an open baseline that can understand telecom industry terminology and reason effectively through telecom operations workflows such as network configuration and customer incident triage. To help operators customize the Nemotron 3 LTM and other open models with their own operational data, NVIDIA released the full recipe that walks through the end-to-end fine-tuning pipeline for adapting open models to operator-specific networks, customers and procedures using NVIDIA NeMo open libraries. Scale Open Models Into Production Workflows Open models are a critical building block, but it takes more than models to bring autonomous telecom operations safely into production. For AT&T, the value of model choice lies in making that flexibility operational in alignment with its business priorities. “At AT&T, we believe the future of AI is not about choosing a single model; it’s about intelligently matching every workload to the right combination of performance, cost and control,” said Andy Markus, chief data and AI officer of AT&T. “Open models are essential to that approach, and with NVIDIA, we can bring that model-choice strategy into production with the scale, reliability and governance our business requires.” Operators need pipelines that prepare and protect their data for model fine‑tuning by anonymizing sensitive records and generating privacy‑preserving synthetic datasets. They also need a platform that can turn open models into governed, autonomous agentic workflows. NVIDIA provides that end-to-end platform , powered by NVIDIA AI Enterprise software and NVIDIA Agent Toolkit , and spanning data pipelines, open models, agent orchestration, secure runtimes and simulation. Together with a strong partner ecosystem building at every layer of this platform, telecom operators have a clear path to translate the benefits of open models into production-ready AI workflows. Create a Platform for Local AI Innovation As telecom operators build AI infrastructure aligned with national AI strategies , open models are giving them a foundation to deliver AI services tailored to local languages, industries, regulations and data governance requirements. Operators across countries can fine-tune open models for local-language and industry-specific needs, as well as host open models on their trusted platforms that customers can consume directly or build on with their own data and applications. For Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, one of Indonesia’s largest telecom operators, that means building AI that reflects the country’s own language and culture through its Sahabat-AI family of open source models. “For countries like Indonesia, the value of open models goes beyond access to powerful AI. It is about adapting that intelligence to our own language, culture, data and real-world needs,” said Chirag Sukhadia, chief data and AI officer of Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison. “Sahabat-AI puts this into practice, using open models as a foundation to build AI that understands Indonesia and can be developed for local applications. This allows us not only to adopt AI, but to build capabilities around it and enable more Indonesians to create with AI on their own terms.” Learn more about NVIDIA technologies for telecommunications . report.one_sentence_summary: ROS 2 기반 대화 제어 및 양팔 용접 프레임워크가 공개되고, EmbeddingGemma 2와 Mistral Large 4 지원 도구 등 온디바이스 및 추론 AI 생태계가 확장되었습니다.
report.cross_insight:
- 해석: Mistral Large 4 API 프리뷰 공개에 맞춰 llm-mistral 0.16 플러그인이 해당 추론 모델 연동을 지원합니다 [11, 13].
- 해석: EmbeddingGemma 2 모델 공개와 Ollama v0.40.0의 지원 추가를 통해 경량 멀티모달 임베딩의 로컬 실행 환경이 연계됩니다 [9, 15, 18].
report.section_robotics:
- **DialoStack**: 파이썬 코드로 대화 흐름과 턴 제어를 확정적으로 관리하고 LLM은 발화 해석과 응답 생성에만 사용하는 ROS 2 오픈소스 패키지로, ROS 2 Jazzy 및 Ubuntu 24.04 소스 빌드와 Gemini 및 Ollama 연동을 지원합니다 [1].
- **Robot Brain**: 작업 실패 지점과 사람의 개입 등 에피소드 경험을 출처와 함께 저장하고 후속 작업에 맞춰 검색하는 비공개 코어 런타임이며, Ubuntu 24.04, Jazzy, ARM64 환경의 ROS 2 DDS 서비스 브리지를 제공합니다 [4].
- **Hold_and_weld v0.3.0**: 전용 지그 없이 한 로봇이 가공물을 잡고 다른 로봇이 용접하도록 지원하는 ROS 2 오픈소스 프레임워크로, CAD·메시 형상 용접선 추출, 제약 조건 기반 파지 샘플링, MoveIt 2 모션 플래닝을 결합하며 ROS 2 Jazzy 및 Ubuntu 24.04를 지원합니다 [5].
report.section_devtools:
- **EmbeddingGemma 2**: Gemma 4 아키텍처 기반의 7억 4천만 파라미터 온디바이스용 경량 멀티모달 오픈 가중치 모델로, Matryoshka Representation Learning을 통해 출력 벡터를 768차원에서 512, 256, 128차원으로 동적 축소할 수 있습니다 [9, 15].
- **llm-mistral 0.16**: LLM CLI 플러그인 릴리스로, 새로 공개된 Mistral Large 4와 같은 신규 추론 모델 지원을 추가했습니다 [11].
- **Mistral Large 4 프리뷰**: 총 1조 개 파라미터, 활성 파라미터 490억 개 규모의 대형 추론 모델 API 프리뷰로, none과 high 두 단계의 추론 레벨 옵션을 제공합니다 [13].
- **Ollama v0.40.0**: Apple Silicon 환경에서 지원 아키텍처를 자동으로 MLX 런타임으로 실행하도록 기본 동작을 변경하고, embeddinggemma-2 등의 모델 지원을 추가했습니다 [18].
- **TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.6**: 작업자 시점의 1인칭 비디오 이해를 지원하여 로보틱스 개발자의 동작 라벨링 및 세분화를 지원하는 AI 모델입니다 [20].

entries.title: DialoStack: ROS 2 기반 결정론적 대화 관리 및 LLM 음성 인터페이스 프레임워크
entries.reason: LLM을 제어 흐름에서 분리하고 파이썬 FSM 기반으로 상태와 회차를 확정적으로 제어하는 HRI 음성 대화 아키텍처를 제공함

facts.statement: DialoStack은 대화 흐름을 상태, 턴 제한, 확인 및 취소 기능을 포함한 파이썬 코드로 구성하고, LLM은 사용자 발화 해석과 응답 생성에만 사용하는 ROS 2 오픈소스 패키지다.
facts.quote: DialoStack, a set of ROS 2 packages where the dialogue flow is plain Python

facts.statement: ROS 2 Jazzy 및 Ubuntu 24.04 환경의 소스 빌드를 지원하며, Gemini 및 Ollama를 통한 로컬 LLM 추론과 슬롯 필링, 설명, 퀴즈 전략을 제공한다.
facts.quote: ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04, built from source.

entries.title: Robot Brain: 태스크 경험 메모리 런타임 및 ROS 2 레퍼런스 브리지
entries.reason: 작업 실패와 인간 개입 이력을 근거와 함께 저장하고 차기 계획 시 검색할 수 있는 런타임 및 ROS 2 DDS 브리지 구조를 설명함

facts.statement: Robot Brain은 작업 실패 지점과 사람의 개입 등을 포함한 에피소드 경험을 사실의 출처와 함께 보존하고 후속 작업 조건에 맞는 기억을 검색하는 비공개 코어 런타임이다.
facts.quote: It keeps task experience (an episode, where it failed, what a human did, what followed)

facts.statement: ROS 2 레퍼런스 브리지는 태스크 수준 DDS 서비스와 영구 요청 큐를 제공하며, Ubuntu 24.04, Jazzy, ARM64 환경에서 검증되었다.
facts.quote: ROS 2 reference bridge: task-level DDS services, a persistent request queue and source-bound private configuration.

entries.title: Hold_and_weld v0.3.0: 양팔 로봇 용접 및 파지 프레임워크
entries.reason: 전용 고정 지그 없이 한 로봇이 공작물을 잡고 다른 로봇이 용접하는 시뮬레이션 기반 양팔 모션 플래닝 파이프라인을 제시함

facts.statement: Hold_and_weld는 한 로봇이 가공물을 잡고 다른 로봇이 용접하여 전용 고정 지그 의존도를 낮추는 것을 목표로 하는 ROS 2 오픈소스 프레임워크다.
facts.quote: an open-source ROS 2 framework for dual-arm robotic welding.

facts.statement: CAD 및 메시 형상 기반 용접선 추출, 제약 조건 기반 파지 샘플링, MoveIt 2 기반 모션 플래닝을 결합하며 ROS 2 Jazzy 및 Ubuntu 24.04를 지원한다.
facts.quote: The framework combines constraint-aware grasp sampling, weld seam extraction from CAD/mesh geometry, and motion planning with MoveIt 2.

entries.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: 온디바이스용 경량 멀티모달 임베딩 모델

facts.statement: EmbeddingGemma 2는 7억 4천만 파라미터 규모로 Gemma 4 아키텍처 기반이며 온디바이스 추론에 최적화된 Apache 2.0 라이선스 멀티모달 모델이다.

facts.statement: Matryoshka Representation Learning(MRL)을 적용하여 출력 벡터를 768차원에서 512, 256, 128차원으로 동적 축소할 수 있다.

selectedItems.title: DialoStack: task-oriented spoken dialogue for ROS 2, with the LLM kept out of the control flow
selectedItems.summary: I’ve been working on getting a robot to run structured spoken conversations, things like a clinic intake (collect name, age, reason for the visit, allergies…), explaining a topic and checking the person understood it, or running a short quiz. Wiring an LLM straight into the speech loop gets you a nice demo quickly, but in my tests it was hard to rely on: it drifted off task, re-asked things it already had, or never decided the conversation was over. So I built DialoStack, a set of ROS 2 packages where the dialogue flow is plain Python (states, turn limits, confirmation, cancellation) and the LLM is only used to interpret what the user said and to phrase the next reply. It started as my bachelor’s thesis, and I presented the work at WAF 2026, the International Workshop on Physical Agents. I’ve put a lot of care into it and I don’t want it to end up as another thesis repo that nobody touches after graduation, so I’m releasing it as open source (MIT) and plan to keep working on it. Wiring an LLM straight into the speech loop gets you a nice demo quickly, but in my tests it was hard to rely on: it drifted off task, re-asked things it already had, or never decided the conversation was over. So I built DialoStack, a set of ROS 2 packages where the dialogue flow is plain Python (states, turn limits, confirmation, cancellation) and the LLM is only used to interpret what the user said and to phrase the next reply. It started as my bachelor’s thesis, and I presented the work at WAF 2026, the International Workshop on Physical Agents. I’ve put a lot of care into it and I don’t want it to end up as another thesis repo that nobody touches after graduation, so I’m releasing it as open source (MIT) and plan to keep working on it. Feedback from people doing HRI would help a lot. 4_captura_gui 1860×990 162 KB A slot-filling task in the web monitor: the frame on the right is filled turn by turn and confirmed before the action returns. Demo on a real NAO (4 min): Dropbox How it’s used Everything goes through one action. You describe the task, and if you don’t pass a schema the engine generates one: ros2 action send_goal --feedback /dialog/execute_task \ ros2_dialog_interfaces/action/DialogTask \ "{task_description: 'Take a coffee order: drink type, size and customer name', dialog_mode: 'slot_filling', domain: 'coffee shop'}" The robot asks for whatever is missing, handles corrections (“actually, make it a large”), confirms, and returns the filled frame as JSON in the result. You can also pass your own schema and a partially filled frame to resume an interrupted dialogue. There is a BehaviorTree.CPP leaf node that wraps the same action. What’s in the repo ros2_dialog_manager : the FSM and three strategies (slot filling, explanation, quiz), with a registry for adding new ones ros2_llm_manager : LLM inference as an action with per-dialogue sessions; Gemini or Ollama behind the same interface, so it can run fully local speech_io : faster-whisper + Silero VAD for STT, Piper for streaming TTS; the mic is muted while the robot speaks vision_io (optional): facial emotion and lip activity, published as topics and added to the prompt context robots/nao : talking gestures and eye-LED feedback, in RViz and on the real robot (via nao_lola) evaluation/ : ROS-free benchmarks against hand-annotated data (slot extraction P/R/F1, intent confusion matrix, quiz grading, simulated end-to-end dialogues) The deterministic core has 173 unit tests that run with plain pytest . Status and limitations ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04, built from source. No binaries yet. You don’t need a robot: a microphone and speakers are enough. Local models via Ollama work and keep all data on the machine, but small ones are noticeably less accurate than Gemini. The only embodiment layer so far is NAO. The core just publishes /is_speaking and /user_vad , so mapping those to another robot should be straightforward, but I haven’t done it. Related work llama_ros and whisper_ros provide LLM and STT inference as ROS 2 nodes, and ROS4HRI defines common HRI interfaces. DialoStack sits a level above those: it’s the dialogue management layer that decides what to ask next and when a task is done. In principle the STT and LLM nodes could be replaced by those packages, though I haven’t tried it yet. Feedback I’m looking for Does a single DialogTask action with a free-text task description feel like the right interface, or would you rather define dialogues declaratively (YAML, BT)? If you work with other social robots (Pepper, TIAGo, …), what would you need from the embodiment layer? Dialogue types you’d use that aren’t covered by slot filling / explanation / quiz. A few issues are tagged good first issue if anyone wants to contribute (an OpenAI-compatible provider, more TTS voices, tests for the quiz and explanation strategies). Bug reports are just as welcome: I’d rather hear what breaks than have it fail quietly on someone’s robot. Repo: GitHub - aquintan4/DialoStack: Task-oriented spoken dialogue for ROS 2 robots. selectedItems.summary: I’m the developer of Robot Brain. I’m posting in Projects because it ships with a ROS 2 reference bridge and I want feedback from people who would actually wire it in. Up front: the core is not open source. It ships as a compiled package under an evaluation license; the repo holds docs, examples and the issue tracker. What it does It keeps task experience (an episode, where it failed, what a human did, what followed) with the source of every fact, and returns what is relevant when a later task asks under its current conditions. With a model key it drafts candidate lessons from that experience, which you review before they are used. New outcomes and counterexamples revise those lessons. Repository hold_and_weld_050 1920×1080 248 KB Constraint-aware grasp sampling The grasp sampler generates antipodal grasp candidates on exact CAD surfaces. Exclusion volumes keep grasps away from weld seams, screw holes and other forbidden regions. Candidates are filtered using gripper geometry and checked for collisions with the workpiece, secondary objects and the ground. STEP and URDF inputs are supported. hold_and_weld_141 1920×1080 220 KB Weld seam extraction The weld finder extracts seams from CAD and mesh geometry and exports weld paths as JSON. The mesh pipeline identifies contact boundaries between parts, traces them along the parts’ edges, and refines the resulting weld paths. hold_and_weld_272 1920×1080 201 KB Weld approach configuration and motion planning Reaching the start of a seam does not necessarily give the robot a suitable configuration for completing the weld. ConfigurationFinder selects the approach joint configuration before OMPL plans the approach. A custom Ceres-based IK solver minimizes position and orientation errors, with hard joint bounds and a seed penalty that favors configurations close to the seed. Multiple initial seeds explore alternative IK branches. Each candidate is evaluated along a sampled Cartesian path covering the plunge and weld motion. IK is solved at each sample using the previous solution as the seed. Candidates are rejected on IK failure, joint-limit violations, low Yoshikawa manipulability or excessive joint steps. Feasible candidates are ranked by their minimum joint-limit margin, minimum manipulability and distance from the home configuration. OMPL plans to the selected configuration as a joint goal. Pilz handles the plunge and linear/circular weld motions; other curves use a dense-waypoint Cartesian fallback. Dual-arm coordination Action servers handle grasping and welding, while a coordinator sequences the workcell: the gripper arm picks and holds the workpiece, then the welding arm executes the weld path. Separate launch files allow either side to run independently. Robot and gripper catalog Models and robot base poses are selected through workcell.yaml . Additional robot and gripper models can be easily integrated through xacro wrappers and catalog registration. A guide documents the required interfaces and configuration steps. Configurator and visualizers The workcell configurator lets you select robot and gripper models and position robots and scene objects using interactive markers in RViz2. Layouts are saved as YAML files, which can be copied into the workcell configuration. Separate visualizers display grasp candidates and weld paths. Testing and current limitations The repository includes unit tests. I also created a complex geometry example with concavities, elliptical surfaces and other geometric features to test grasp sampling and seam extraction. Results look good on the tested examples; additional geometry testing would help assess broader coverage. The complete workflow has been demonstrated in simulation. It has not yet been validated through physical welding trials. Existing physical demonstrations show that robot-held welding is feasible at smaller scales too. I’m actively working toward a hardware demonstration of this framework. The roadmap outlines planned development. Sahil Dua Research Engineer, Google DeepMind Henrique Schechter Vera Research Engineer, Google DeepMind Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X We introduced EmbeddingGemma last year to provide a lightweight option for high-quality text embeddings, to help your apps organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware. The developer community’s response blew past our expectations. With more than 20 million downloads, builders have used it to power smarter on-device search tools and privacy-first retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipelines. Today, we’re launching EmbeddingGemma 2, expanding beyond text to unify code, images, video, and audio in a shared embedding space. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license, EmbeddingGemma 2 has 740 million parameters, making it optimal for on-device inference. It can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model. Built from the same technology as Gemini Embedding models, EmbeddingGemma 2 is: Best-in-class for its size: Achieves leading scores among sub-1B multimodal embedders for its size across benchmarks like MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) Code and MAEB (Massive Audio Embedding Benchmark), while matching or outperforming many larger models across text, vision, and audio tasks. Modular by design: Requires as little as 270M parameters for text-only workloads with optional vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders for full multimodal support. Storage-efficient: Using Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), developers can dynamically truncate output vectors from 768 dimensions down to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions. This provides up to 6x storage reduction for local vector databases and memory usage. Optimized for on-device performance: Runs efficiently within tight resource constraints. With quantization, on a Google Pixel 11 Pro, EmbeddingGemma 2 requires as little as ~191MB active RAM for text-only weights and ~567MB for the full multimodal model. Extended context ready: Features an 8K token context window (4x larger than EmbeddingGemma 1), allowing it to process up to 5.5 minutes of audio, 29 images, 58 video frames, or interleaved combinations thereof directly on local hardware. Achieving top-tier quality for code, vision, and audio EmbeddingGemma 2 matches the strong multilingual text performance of EmbeddingGemma while delivering a significant 9.92-point improvement on code performance (in MTEB Code, from 68.76 to 78.68), making it well-suited for local codebase indexing, semantic code search, and coding agent retrieval. Across image, video, documents, and audio, it sets a new standard in quality-per-parameter for sub-1B models and even outperforms some specialist models more than twice its size. Find full evaluation metrics and model information in the EmbeddingGemma 2 model card . Enabling semantic search, routing, and retrieval, fully on-device EmbeddingGemma 2 brings robust capabilities directly to edge hardware. Generating embeddings locally helps ensure data privacy, reduces pipeline latency, and empowers developers to build cross-modal search and retrieval that works entirely offline. When paired with generative models such as Gemma 4, EmbeddingGemma 2 enables on-device RAG pipelines that understand complex multimodal data. Because EmbeddingGemma 2 is built on Gemma 4 and shares its text tokenizer and audio encoder, developers can run both models together in a unified pipeline with a lower combined total memory footprint. Use text or an image to find the top matches in your media library based on semantic similarity. Try it in Google AI Edge Gallery ’s Instant Media Search. Locate specific moments in video using text or audio queries. Try it in Google AI Edge Gallery ’s Video Moments Finder. Pair EmbeddingGemma 2 for local file retrieval with Gemma 4 for contextual reasoning. Try it in the Google AI Edge Foresight app. Create real-time decision engines leveraging multimodal context for classification, routing, and predictive capabilities via the MediaPipe Decision Task API . To learn how to build on-device search and RAG systems with LiteRT, read the Google AI Edge blog post . Visit LiteRT Community on Hugging Face for models optimized for on-device. Build for the browser with transformers.js or WebGPU .
